reviews.frank_statement: FRANK should be researched as a hierarchical multiscale recurrent loop-of-loops and ClayCode should represent recurrent state, timescale, budget, halt, dynamics, intervention and rollback semantics.
reviews.counterhypothesis: The runtime can represent loop families using generic typed state/functions/control flow and explicit scheduling data; a first-class loop language primitive is unnecessary.
reviews.falsifier: Production compiler/runtime evidence showing generic typed control-flow cannot preserve required loop behavior, timescales, rollback or safety while a dedicated loop semantic primitive can.
independent_checks: Current-run randomized executable schedule/effect/capability experiment: 30,000 coupled schedules, 50,000 effect call-graphs, 30,000 capability cases.
Microsoft P primary research: asynchronous systems can be expressed as interacting state machines with compiled executable semantics and verification.
Bauer/Pretnar and Koka primary literature: effect sets can be tracked in type/effect systems rather than inferred from prose.
WASI capability design: external authority is granted by capabilities/handles, not by textual effect naming.
adversarial_checks: Permuted loop schedules under sequential coupled updates.
Same permutations under synchronous snapshot aggregation.
Textual/forged capability claim without valid capability grant.
reviews.reason: The loop-of-loops modeling pressure is real, but it does not independently justify new loop syntax. The executable counterexample instead requires explicit schedule/update policy in semantic identity and transitive effect closure. Existing Ordered<T>, records/state plus already-required general control-flow/function closure appear sufficient until production evidence falsifies that economy.
reviews.claycode_action: Prioritize production control-flow/type-effect/evaluator closure; encode schedule policy explicitly and preserve ordered schedule identity for sequential semantics; do not add a first-class loop primitive now.
